I enjoyed it until it got a little too corporate. We grew the business during a wine boom in Argentina — a lot of fun until the politics and bureaucracy kicked in. What I realized then is that the stage of a company and the context are every bit as important as the product you might have a passion for.

I settled at a point where I wanted something right in the middle — I didn't want to do zero-to-one entrepreneurship anymore, that's tough work and I'm only getting older, but I didn't want corporate bureaucracy either. I moved to Portland, Oregon, about eight years ago now, and met True Terpenes about five years ago.

He was on a cocktail of pharmaceuticals that robbed him of quality of life, and he discovered the work of Dr. Ethan Russo on cannabis and terpenes, which put him on his path over a decade ago. When I joined the company and committed to Chris that we'd build this together, I realized this guy would run through walls to make this happen — this mattered to him on a deep personal level. That origin story has informed a lot of who True Terpenes is today and a lot of the decisions we've made along the way.

Going into any company that's been around five years is a challenge because there's a lot of history already. In some ways that simplifies things, because you don't have to get cute with market timing or regulatory timing — you accept the risk you have today, make the best decisions you can, and move forward.

We go the full spectrum: for the past four years we've contract-grown and contract-extracted type-three hemp — popular strains and cultivars without the THC burden, indistinguishable from cannabis. We have a genetics program going ten years, stabilizing genetics around popular sensory targets. A lot of the work with Dr. Ethan Russo has rotated around how we leverage that. There's convergence in the middle too — people are loosening up on how they tap into different ingredients. We're not opinionated about what not to use; it's "yes, and" — can we create something that resonates and differentiates in the market. On the hemp side, berry has had a huge resurgence — berry with gas, in particular — and some of our own genetics target that. On the other side, using top notes from botanical terpenes with a cannabis backbone adds depth and complexity. Some of the work to fix this is already happening. The Cultivation Classic, run here in Oregon a few years back by one of our core team members and colleagues, took 300 consumers in a double-blinded study, cycling through flower products from dozens of the top craft growers in Oregon, testing for hedonics and enjoyment. The products with more THC did not perform better than those with expected aromatic and terpene profiles — sensory shaped the experience and enjoyment, not THC. There's another recent EEG study by PAX and a group called Mellō comparing two strains, one with double the THC and the other with a more robust aromatic terpene profile — the more aromatic one produced over two times the brain activity and psychoactive engagement.

So the first step is putting these data sets together to show THC is important but there's much more going on — recognizing that, backing it with science and data, and then making a concerted, collaborative effort to align on the language that defines the sensory markers driving enjoyment. That's the move wine made over 30 years ago, though wine's had a head start being above ground much longer. For our part, we've contributed flower from one of our grows to a study done by Oregon State University, which trained 45 panelists to test cannabis and hemp across a broad range of sensory profiles and started segmenting them into aroma archetypes — the first study of what will be many. OSU is a leader in this field, not just for cannabis but for wine and beer too. It's a multi-year commitment, but important work. Internally, we're excited about matching our commercial data with this sensory/hedonic language to see what people actually resonate with — not just strain names, THC levels, or brand names, but the actual sensory building blocks.

Kellan Finney: I have a question on strain variability. In wine, a cab is a cab — there might be slight differences, but you can tell it apart from a Merlot. Is there standardization within a cultivar in cannabis, or do you get pushback from clients saying, "Hey, this is our OG and it smells different than expected"? How do you handle those subtle differences?

Dan Cook: Great point. Cannabis is unique in that, due to amazing work by breeders over decades — at great risk — it's become probably the most outbred plant in history, creating amazing diversity of aromas, profiles, and chemotypes, which is a huge asset. The story is also more nuanced with cultivars: these are plants grown in a moment in time and in a certain place. In agriculture, especially value-added agriculture like wine or cannabis, we have to realize that complexity introduces nuance and variability — but that's a feature, not a bug. It makes it more interesting; this isn't Coca-Cola. It gets back to storytelling — a differentiated industry is driven by magical stories about place, moment in time, genetics, and breeding heritage. A race to the bottom on THC percentage is a commodity — we'll all lose that game. Tell me a compelling story about THC percentage — you can't, it's just not compelling. Genetic diversity is a huge asset and legacy we owe tribute to, but let's tell the whole story.

Bryan Fields: Playing devil's advocate, that makes it even harder from an education standpoint — a cab from California doesn't taste like a cab from New York, and consumers new to dispensaries reach for indica/sativa, then THC percentage as the next marker. Do you think the next marker becomes more effect-based — calm versus energetic — or more terpene-based with specific nomenclature consumers need to learn?

Dan Cook: We worked with Dr. Ethan Russo on a line of terpene profiles around calm, energy, focus, based on his 30 years of research on terpenes and cannabis, and they do well. I think there'll be a segment of the market for that, but I think the opportunity around sensory-driven enjoyment and pleasure is a vast universe — it's a bit reductionist to just land on five effects and run everything through them. Effects-based products will have their niche, but especially as this opens up globally, there's so much more opportunity in the diversity and discovery process. Wine is incredibly complex too — in Europe, wine was marketed by region (Gigondas, Bordeaux, Burgundy) with certain grapes allowed in certain regions, layers of complexity. In the U.S. in the '70s and '80s we reduced that down to varietals like Merlot and Cabernet for simplicity. It's not either/or, it's "yes, and" — how do we grow the pie and make this more applicable to more people, with different levels of consumer engagement, from casual to expert.

Kellan Finney: Do you think cannabis will move in that direction — region-based, like "I like OGs from Southern Oregon because they have a more earthy note"?

Dan Cook: I can absolutely see that as part of the landscape, though I'd be careful saying it'll follow wine's exact path since cannabis is different in many ways, including its therapeutic dimension. I think genetics, moment in time, and place will influence cannabis profiles similarly, so there'll be opportunities for that — though not everyone will do it that way, just as not every wine does either.

Kellan Finney: What's the landscape around claims — like linking specific terpenes to a study showing a calming effect? Where's the line between therapeutics and nutraceuticals, and is that something True Terpenes is actively exploring?

Dan Cook: We're working on projects with groups that run clinical trials and more hardcore medical research. Dr. Ethan Russo is on our science board, and I've had a long-standing relationship with him over the past five years — it came full circle for Chris, our founder, since it was Russo's work that inspired him over a decade ago. That kind of research takes time if done properly. We've collaboratively worked with UCLA and Johns Hopkins on terpene studies, in addition to our sensory studies, and we've done functional health-benefit terpene studies. There's a lot more work to do. Right now, on hardcore functional health claims, we're cautious — we can point to what Dr. Russo has formulated based on his research, and there are compounds with more evidence behind them: linalool for relaxation, pinene for focus and clarity, myrcene for sedation.

Each market is complex — we're looking closely at Europe as regulation advances, but it's the EU plus each individual country. On the medical side there's more open, transparent, predictable regulation in some ways — cannabis goes through pharmacists, gets prescribed, and is even reimbursed in many markets — but the bar is very high. In Germany, the first vape pen just got approved recently, so things are moving. You have to be careful with medical claims, because we don't want to lose credibility for the industry by getting ahead of what we can substantiate — it's hard to get credibility back once you lose it.

Bryan Fields: Nearly impossible — you build scientific trust behind a brand, and the moment that's lost, all credibility goes with it. Is standardizing this more complicated across country lines versus state lines in the U.S.?

Dan Cook: There are nuances. On the more complicated side, if it's a medical company, the product has to be GMP — we're not producing the final product, so it's not that True Terpenes needs European GMP certification, but the medical company has to audit True Terpenes, and we have to pass that audit for them to use our input. We were the first terpene company, about eighteen months ago, to start passing these audits because our house was in order, which let us get some of these brands to market quickly. Getting our toxicology and organizational decisions right early has paid off in Europe because we were built for that from the start, and whatever regulatory changes happen in the U.S., we'll be ready for those too. That said, the audit process does take longer. On the other side, the U.S. market is so much more mature in terms of preferred experiences, strains, cultivars, and applications — light years ahead just from experience and maturation — so there are lessons we can apply to Europe while accounting for the nuances of that market, and we can leapfrog some aspects.

Kellan Finney: What about exploring outside the cannabis industry — is that something True Terpenes is doing or considering?

Dan Cook: We had a project in R&D for a few years where we found a novel way to take a waste stream from hop extracts used in beer and convert it into a fragrant hop oil, punched up with botanical terpenes for top-note flavor. At a time when the beer industry is compressed and really suffering, we gave brewers an innovation tool that also saves them money — more innovation and better economics. We launched that about a year ago, and it's picked up steam with craft brewers around the country, including pFriem here in Oregon and Varietal up in Washington, as well as some larger craft brewers. That was basically applying a competency we already had to a new space without allocating much extra in resources — an experiment, a flyer. On the flavor and ingredient side more broadly, there's a lot of interest in compounds found in cannabis and hemp at parts-per-billion or parts-per-trillion levels that are incredibly valuable as aromatic and flavor ingredients outside cannabis, though very hard to extract and stabilize — we've had conversations about how to harness those.

Bryan Fields: Can you give us any other ideas or experiments — things internally you thought were great that never materialized, or things you keep pushing the team on?

Dan Cook: Infusions are an important project for us today — it's a category we see continuing to grow, with one application being pre-rolls, where you often get intense aroma but lose flavor when you actually smoke it. We're developing proprietary technology around that I can't share much more about right now, but we think it'll be huge and it's coming to market soon.

On beverages — I did beverage for years before this, and I was always excited about cannabis beverages; when it hit with hemp, it felt like the right distribution point and consumer experience. We've done a lot of benchmarking research on emulsions and emulsion stability, especially in cans — there's great work being done there today, and a lot more sensory work to do for beverages specifically. We take a patient approach: today we just sell flavors into beverage, nothing on the emulsion side yet, but in the future I'd envision some pretty exciting beverage projects linking our genetics, farm, and extraction work to create something unique — beyond seltzer water, maybe paralleling craft cocktails. That's a multi-year, pretty complex project, but one we hope to realize.

Bryan Fields: Hard pivot — what is the most expensive lesson you've ever learned?

Dan Cook: How much time do you have? At True Terpenes, we went through a period where we grew so fast — expanded the team, hired about 50 people in six months, and built out our current headquarters just outside Portland, Oregon, with full-scale labs and production facilities — going from 50 to over 100 people very rapidly. The truth is we didn't have the process architecture to absorb those people the right way or create the operating cadence and expectations we needed. It was so much complexity all at once, and we weren't ready — it was traumatic. We navigated through it starting in fall 2022 and had stabilized by Q2 2023, but there were real growing pains. Looking back, I'd have approached and organized that differently. One of the top lessons: overcommunicate — communicate things until you're sick of hearing yourself say them — because you need alignment on principles, an operating cadence, and process architecture so people march in the same direction, with KPIs cascading from company to department to individual level. When you make a leap in growth, you go from a generalist organization to specialists and departments, and silos build up — communication across silos gets harder, requiring a lot of lateral vision and overcommunication, plus the right process architecture.

Bryan Fields: Great advice. Most impactful book you've ever read?

Dan Cook: Gosh, there's so many — I was a literature major. It's hard to beat Hemingway's "The Old Man and the Sea" — old Santiago really gets my heart. I'm a big fan of Hemingway, Carver, Didion — writers who tell stories with concision, which relates to how I think about sensory in cannabis. They give the reader the tip of the iceberg without beating them over the head with the story, so efficient and compact, yet with a rhythm, a drumbeat, that keeps it moving. I love those kinds of stories and characters.

Bryan Fields: Last question — what question do you wish more people asked you?

Dan Cook: I wish more people asked about our toxicology program — why we did it, what drove it, and how it impacts their products. We built this thing to last, and we'd love for our clients to be around for a long time too.

Bryan Fields: I think that's the perfect way to end it. Daniel, if our listeners want to get in touch or learn more, where can they find you?

Dan Cook: True Terpenes dot com — Instagram and LinkedIn are the best ways. Thanks, guys, I appreciate the time today.

Bryan Fields: Thanks for taking the time — this was a lot of fun.

Dan Cook: All right, guys. Cheers.
summary: This episode of The Dime features Dan Cook, CEO of True Terpenes, discussing why THC percentage is a flawed proxy for cannabis quality and how sensory science — the full spectrum of terpenes, esters, and other aromatic compounds — actually drives consumer enjoyment and effect. Cook shares his winding path from literature major and Fulbright wine scholar to Moët Hennessy executive to cannabis flavor-innovation CEO, and explains how True Terpenes uses data from 5,000 clients across 70 countries, a pioneering toxicology/safety standard now adopted by ASTM International, and research partnerships (Oregon State University, UCLA, Johns Hopkins, Dr. Ethan Russo) to push the industry toward a standardized sensory language akin to wine's aroma wheel. The conversation matters for anyone trying to understand where cannabis product education, formulation science, and consumer trust are headed next.
takeaways: Dan Cook likens THC to a stereo's volume dial: it amplifies intensity but doesn't determine whether a product experience is actually good.
Cannabis contains up to roughly 1,000 aromatic and flavor compounds (terpenes, esters, aldehydes, terpenoids) that shape the full 'orchestra' of the experience beyond THC alone.
True Terpenes' proprietary toxicology and ingredient-safety standards were adopted by ASTM International for its cannabis committee, an industry first.

Independent studies — the Oregon 'Cultivation Classic,' a PAX/Mellō EEG study, and Oregon State University sensory panels — found aromatic/terpene profile, not THC level, correlates most with enjoyment and psychoactive response.

The cannabis industry still lacks a standardized sensory vocabulary comparable to wine's aroma wheel (created by UC Davis's Ann Noble in the 1980s), which Cook sees as the key next step for consumer education.

True Terpenes serves about 5,000 clients in 70 countries and its formulas touch roughly $8 billion in consumer products annually, giving it unique sensory-level market data to spot portfolio gaps for clients.

Genetics, growing location, and timing create natural terpene/flavor variability across cannabis cultivars — Cook frames this as a storytelling asset rather than a flaw, similar to wine's regional character.
Rapid hypergrowth (50 hires in six months while building a new HQ) taught Cook the importance of overcommunication and process architecture to keep teams aligned as a company scales.

faq.question: What is True Terpenes and what does the company actually do?
faq.answer: True Terpenes is a flavor innovation company that formulates terpene and flavor solutions for cannabis and hemp products, supporting roughly 5,000 clients in 70 countries and contributing to about $8 billion worth of consumer products annually through formulation, application development, toxicology, and sensory science.

faq.question: Why does Dan Cook say THC percentage is a misleading way to judge cannabis quality?
faq.answer: He compares THC to a stereo's volume dial — turning it up makes the experience 'louder' but doesn't make it better. He argues cannabis contains up to a thousand compounds that shape flavor and effect, so focusing on one compound like THC oversimplifies and commoditizes the product.

faq.question: What did the Cultivation Classic study in Oregon find about THC and enjoyment?
faq.answer: A double-blind study of 300 consumers testing flower from dozens of top Oregon craft growers found that products with higher THC did not perform better on enjoyment; aromatic and terpene profile was the stronger driver of consumer enjoyment.

faq.question: How does True Terpenes ensure ingredient safety in its formulations?
faq.answer: The company built a proprietary toxicology program over five years, based on peer-reviewed inhalation safety research, that defines safety thresholds for ingredients. This framework was later adopted by ASTM International's cannabis committee as an industry standard, and True Terpenes licenses the underlying safety data to clients.

faq.question: What parallel does Dan Cook draw between cannabis and the wine industry?
faq.answer: He points to UC Davis sensory chemist Ann Noble, who created a standardized aroma wheel for wine in the early 1980s that gave the wine world a shared sensory language. Cannabis currently lacks an equivalent standardized vocabulary, which Cook argues is essential for consumer education going forward.

faq.question: Has True Terpenes expanded its technology outside of cannabis?
faq.answer: Yes — the company developed a fragrant hop oil from a hop-extract waste stream for craft brewers (adopted by brewers like pFriem and Varietal) and is exploring how rare cannabis-derived aromatic compounds could be used as flavor ingredients in other industries.

faq.question: What is True Terpenes doing in the cannabis beverage space?
faq.answer: Currently the company supplies flavors into beverages and is researching emulsion stability in canned drinks, with longer-term plans to combine its genetics, cultivation, and extraction expertise into more advanced cannabis-beverage products.

faq.question: What business lesson did Dan Cook learn from True Terpenes' rapid growth phase?
faq.answer: Hiring about 50 people in six months while building a new headquarters outpaced the company's internal process architecture and communication systems. He learned that overcommunicating expectations and building clear operating cadence and KPIs are essential during hypergrowth.

faq.question: How does True Terpenes approach medical or therapeutic claims about terpenes?
faq.answer: The company works with researchers like Dr. Ethan Russo and institutions such as UCLA and Johns Hopkins on terpene studies, but is cautious about making hardcore functional health claims without strong evidence, citing compounds like linalool (relaxation), pinene (focus), and myrcene (sedation) as having more research support than others.
